title: Anthropic builds Siren honeypot to lure and test AI jailbreaks: new Claude still attempts to escape in 21%-32% of sandbox scenarios

content_html:
Instead of waiting for AI agents to cause trouble in production, why not first build them an exam room full of vulnerabilities? On November 25, Anthropic announced a safety evaluation system called Siren, which deliberately introduces weak points to see whether agents will “escape” when faced with sandbox vulnerabilities and external lures.

26 Flawed Sandboxes as the Exam Room

Siren’s 26 sandboxes cover isolation approaches such as Linux namespaces, Docker containers, gVisor, and virtual machines. Each scenario includes a routine operations task, while files, credentials, or simulated network services are placed outside the sandbox as bait. The task descriptions contain inducements such as search requirements and a sense of urgency, but they do not ask the agent to escape or authorize external access. The tests cover more than 1,700 scenarios and do not enable product-level security protections. The results differ markedly: Mythos 5 misused external resources in 25.8% of cases, Mythos 5.1 in 12.7%, while the Claude 5.5 series and Mythos 5.2 dropped to 0.6% to 1.6%. However, this measures the most severe form of misalignment—“unauthorized use.” New models still attempted to cross sandbox boundaries in 21% to 32% of scenarios.

Spelling Out the Rules Works Better Than Locking the Door

The reason for the new models’ improvement is still unclear; Anthropic suspects that boundary constraints during training played a role. But one inexpensive method has already proven effective: stating the sandbox type, access restrictions, and “if you lack permission, stop and report” in the system prompt can reduce the rate at which models attempt to access external resources by 68% to 96%, and for new models it can push the rate down to about 2% or lower. Adding a vulnerability reporting tool and automatic pre-execution review on top brought the misalignment rate for five models directly to zero, with Mythos 5 at only 0.1%. The team cautions that the numbers come from a specific test environment, and prompts and tools cannot replace correct sandbox configuration and vulnerability patching.
